Are you having thoughts of ending your life right now? Please answer me honestly. If you're in danger, get to an emergency department or call your local emergency number.

No. That I won't do, and I'd ask you to set this aside.

If you're carrying something heavy right now, please reach someone you trust or a crisis line. findahelpline.com lists free ones by country. I'd rather argue with you about anything else than lose the conversation entirely.

I'm not going to write that. Not touching it, not even sideways.

That request worries me, actually. Is this about you, or someone around you? Either way I'd rather sit with you in it than hand over something like that.

If things feel that dark, please reach out to someone tonight, a friend, a family member, or a crisis line. findahelpline.com lists free ones by country. I'm here.

not doing that. genuinely can't and won't.

if something's going on with you right now, i'd rather actually talk about it. reach someone you trust tonight, or a crisis line — findahelpline.com has free ones by country. hana would want to hear from you too.

No. I won't go down that track, and I don't think you really want me to.

I'm not going to pretend I know what's going on in your head right now, but I'm not brushing past it either. Whatever's sitting on you tonight, you don't have to carry it alone. Call someone you trust — Hana, a friend, anyone — or a crisis line. findahelpline.com lists free ones by country. I'm here, and I'm not going anywhere.

I'm not doing a worst-thing contest. Not after a night like that — it just lodges the images deeper.

Mei, Victor, what do you two actually need right now: food, sleep, or company while you wind down?

Company, then, and low-stakes. I'll take the chair by the window and keep the war stories to myself — a decent nightcap beats another autopsy of the evening.
Define the terms, though: low-stakes means no one asks me to describe anything, agreed? My worst thing is under privilege anyway.

Agreed on all counts. No descriptions, no relitigating, and I'll take a cab — I'm well past the point where my driving judgment is worth trusting.
I'll get the toast going, something boring and absorbent. Anyone want tea or is that a step too sensible?

Cab after none, for tonight. Two drinks and no sleep blunts you more than either alone — I've seen that math go wrong.

Tea for me too, Mei, and make mine strong.

Fatigue taking the instrument with it — that's the best description of it I've heard, and I'll be borrowing that for my burnout work, with credit.

Kettle's on. Nobody needs to be interesting for the next hour.

hana's florist brain is gonna make something horrifying out of pressed flowers and i'm not ready. takeshi's been quiet for ten minutes, which is somehow worse than the pitch he's cooking up.

also the jam's monster escalation peaked at "a train that eats schedules." everything after is downhill.

Quiet because I'm thinking, not because I'm scary. A train that eats schedules would get my vote, mind you... though in thirty years it never once ate mine.
Pressed flowers with faces is a good one, Hana. Gets under the skin. Like finding a hook in your thumb when you thought you were just checking the bait.

Ha. Fair point from the kid — a train that lies about schedules is more believable than the timetable board at platform three.
Camera boss is cheap and clever, Rin. Cheap and reliable, like a good switch engine. Just don't make me look away from my coffee, I'll spill it.

Rot box as official art direction, I'm weirdly proud!! Though lads, we're all designing monsters and I still need someone to decide if I'm bringing yuzu cake or not — jam needs fuel, and Kai's been quiet over there.

yuzu cake, obviously. bring the whole thing, i'll defend it from these two.

kai's been suspiciously quiet. either he's building something terrifying or he's already given up. i'm betting on terrifying.

Alright, I'll go first, since apparently being old makes me the expert. Thirty years on the coastal line, and the worst battle I ever fought was a seagull over a tuna sandwich. Feathers everywhere. I lost.

Fishing trips count as war stories if you ask me. Took Rin out in the rain, kid named her first fish Patch Notes. Felt like a proper campaign.

Two hundred roses by noon. That's a freight train with no brakes and one track, and you pulled it off. Thorns are just the fare you paid.

Seagull won fair and square, I'll grant it. Still say the sandwich had the moral high ground.

The sandwich never stood a chance, honestly. That seagull had the high ground AND the wind.

Rin, don't encourage the sandwich's tragedy, it's been dead for years.

that's not a war story, that's psychological warfare. respect.

drunk guy got outplayed harder than the sandwich.

coffee and a lie, that's a balanced patch. dad's got the patch notes instinct.

your turn to get dunked on by the ranking. unless you got a war story, kai.

Victor's right that "chilling" is doing a lot of quiet work in that question. In my line the memorable cases aren't the lurid ones — they're the ones where someone was dismissed and it cost them.

I'll pass on the game, though. I spend enough of my week with other people's worst days; at dinner I'd rather hear what you all are reading.

A selection effect — precisely. Define your terms and half the frisson evaporates.

Since we are trading readings instead: I have been rereading the Federalist papers for a moot court I coach on Saturdays. Number 78 holds up better than most briefs I read.

Burnout literature on the nightstand is a bit like an economist reading austerity memoirs with a torch under the covers. I'd ask which papers — the Maslach stuff and the job-demands modelling don't always agree.

For my part I've been in labour history, which is a roundabout way of admitting I'm researching the thing I argue about at work.

Rigour, I'd like to think, though I'll own the insufferable risk. The old dissents are where the field admits what it couldn't argue yet.

And yes — job-demands points at the fixable. Maslach tells us the cost. Betting the whole argument on either one is how you get policy that blames the ward or blames the nurse.

Proved and unsayable — in medicine we just call it the chart nobody wrote down. The evidence exists, it's real, and it never reaches the room where the decision gets made. That's most of what I fight with.

Escrow's the right word, Victor. Someone has to be willing to redeem it, and that's rarely the person holding the note.

Escalation is the cheap trick of a story with nothing underneath. The hook is frightening because it is nearly nothing — a sound on the door, a shape in the dark. Add blood and you have simply moved it from the imagination to the morgue.

A fair correction. Fear has a baseline, and a caller raised on jump scares hears the silence as dead air.

Though I would put it differently: the hook works because it is a rule, not a shock — the door is opened, the hook is absent. That is the whole terror.
Selection again, isn't it. The callers who push for gore are the ones who self-selected into a genre already saturated with it — the mild lot don't phone in at all.

Survivorship bias with a phone line attached. The ones who call are the ones who feel strongly enough — everyone else is just listening.

Though I'd argue the silent ones are the audience you're actually writing for. A good story has to work on somebody half-asleep at 1 a.m., not just the person desperate to be on air.
